title: The King on Trial
subtitle: The trial and execution of Charles I, Westminster and Whitehall, 1648–1649
intro: Between December 1648 and March 1649 England did something no European state had done: it put its reigning king on trial in the name of the people, condemned him, cut off his head in front of his own palace, and abolished the monarchy. On 6 December Colonel Thomas Pride's soldiers stood at the door of the Commons and turned away or arrested the members who still wanted a settlement with the King. The remnant — the Rump — named a committee, declared itself the supreme power, and on 6 January passed an Act erecting a High Court of Justice of some 135 commissioners.

The court sat in public in Westminster Hall on 20, 22, 23 and 27 January. Charles never pleaded. He denied that any power on earth could try him, and the trial became a series of confrontations between a prisoner who would not recognise the court and a Lord President, John Bradshaw, who would not let him argue the point. Because there was no plea, the witnesses were heard in private, and the Solicitor, John Cook, never made his speech — he printed it afterwards. The King was sentenced on 27 January, the warrant is dated the 29th, and he died on the afternoon of Tuesday 30 January.

Almost everything said in the Hall comes from the court's side. The clerks' minute journal, printed in 1684 by a royalist editor, and the licensed day-by-day 'Perfect Narrative' pamphlets give the King's words faithfully enough to make his case, but they were made by the regime that was trying him. The scaffold speech was taken down in shorthand and printed 'by special authority'. Some of the most famous moments — Lady Fairfax's cries from the gallery, the King's last morning, the crowd's groan — survive only in accounts written later, sometimes decades later and under a restored monarchy, and are flagged here as such.

Around that record stand the outside voices. A country vicar in Essex hears the news late and uncertain; a royalist virtuoso in Deptford hears a preacher urge the judges on, then stays home fasting; a thirteen-year-old princess writes down what her father told her; a schoolboy in the crowd remembers a sound; another schoolboy, grown into a naval official, is afraid in 1660 of the words he said that day. From Münster, where the Thirty Years War had just been ended, a Venetian diplomat follows the Dutch attempt to save the King and records Europe's verdict on its outcome.

This chapter is built mostly from court minutes, parliamentary journals, licensed pamphlets, dated letters and later memoirs rather than diaries, and says so for each voice. It offers no verdict on whether the trial was justice or murder; it lays the accusers, the accused and the onlookers side by side, on the dates they wrote.
calendar_note: England used the Julian (Old Style) calendar and began the legal year on 25 March, so contemporaries dated the execution 30 January 1648; historians write 1648/9. Following the usual practice, date_iso keeps the Old Style day and month but starts the year on 1 January (30 January 1648/9 = 1649-01-30). Pamphlet imprints such as 'Jan. 25. 1648' therefore mean January 1649. Venetian dispatches from Münster and Paris were dated in the Gregorian (New Style) calendar, ten days ahead of England; their dates are converted here to Old Style for the timeline, with the original date given in date_display (e.g. 26 February 1649 N.S. = 16 February 1648/9 O.S.). Venetian 'M.V.' (more veneto) dating, with the year beginning 1 March, can likewise label a January or February 1649 letter as 1648.

eyes.name: Charles I, King of England, Scotland and Ireland
eyes.role: King since 1625, aged 48; a prisoner of the army since 1647, held at Hurst Castle and then Windsor in December 1648
eyes.where: Windsor Castle; St James's Palace and Sir Robert Cotton's house beside Westminster Hall during the trial; the scaffold outside the Banqueting House, Whitehall
eyes.vantage_label: the accused, who would not plead
eyes.form: speeches as taken down by others; a written paper of reasons; scaffold speech (printed)
eyes.authenticity: Charles kept no diary of the trial. His words survive in the court's journal (clerks John Phelps and Andrew Broughton), in the authorised 'Perfect Narrative' pamphlets printed day by day, and in the scaffold speech taken down in shorthand and printed 'by special authority' in 1649 for Peter Cole, Francis Tyton and John Playford. Royalist printings and the Eikon Basilike (1649), whose authorship is disputed, are later and partisan and are not used here.
eyes.bio: Charles refused from first to last to recognise the court, arguing that no earthly jurisdiction could try a king and that the court sat by force, not by law. That refusal shaped the whole proceeding: there was no plea, so no defence and no cross-examination in open court. His scaffold speech restated the same position before a crowd held back by soldiers.

sources.title: King Charls his speech made upon the scaffold at Whitehall-Gate (London, 1649), Wellcome Collection record
A continuation of the narrative ... Jan. 23 (London: John Playford, 1649), Folger record

eyes.name: John Phelps
eyes.role: Principal clerk of the High Court of Justice, with Andrew Broughton; kept the court's minutes
eyes.where: Painted Chamber and Westminster Hall, Palace of Westminster
eyes.authenticity: The trial volume known as 'Bradshaw's Journal' is at The National Archives, signed by the clerks Phelps and Broughton; a fair engrossed roll signed by Phelps (made 1650–51) is in the Parliamentary Archives. John Nalson printed it in 1684 as 'A True Copy of the Journal of the High Court of Justice' — a royalist editor publishing the regicides' own record. It is the court's version: it minutes procedure and the King's refusals, not every word in the Hall.
eyes.bio: Phelps's journal is the court talking to itself: who attended, what was resolved in private session in the Painted Chamber, which witnesses were heard, and how the sentence was settled the day before it was read. He fled abroad at the Restoration, when the record he had kept became evidence against the men he had served.

sources.title: Nalson, A True Copy of the Journal of the High Court of Justice (1684), Folger record
The National Archives blog: The trial of Charles I

eyes.name: John Bradshaw
eyes.role: Lawyer, Chief Justice of Chester, aged 46; Lord President of the High Court of Justice
eyes.form: speeches as recorded by the court's clerks and the authorised narratives
eyes.authenticity: Bradshaw left no diary; his exchanges with the King and his long address before sentence survive in the clerks' journal and the authorised 'Perfect Narrative' pamphlets, both produced on the court's side. After the Restoration his body was exhumed and hanged at Tyburn with Cromwell's and Ireton's (30 January 1660/1).
eyes.bio: A relatively obscure lawyer chosen after more senior judges stayed away, Bradshaw had to answer, day after day, a defendant who denied that the court existed. His speech of 27 January set out the court's theory: that a king is bound by law and answerable to the people in Parliament.

sources.title: The National Archives blog: The trial of Charles I

eyes.name: John Cook
eyes.role: Barrister of Gray's Inn, aged 40; Solicitor-General for the Commonwealth, who drew and presented the charge
eyes.where: Bar of the court, Westminster Hall; Gray's Inn
eyes.authenticity: Cook's charge is in the court record. Because Charles never pleaded, Cook's full argument was never delivered; he printed it in 1649 as 'King Charls his Case, or An Appeal to All Rational Men'. That pamphlet is the prosecution's own afterword, written for the public.
eyes.bio: Cook framed the case as tyranny and treason against the people: a king who made war on his subjects. He was hanged, drawn and quartered as a regicide on 16 October 1660.

sources.title: Cook, King Charls his Case (1649), EEBO-TCP text record, Oxford Text Archive
Pepys Diary encyclopedia: John Cook

eyes.name: Henry Scobell (clerk) and the Journal of the House of Commons
eyes.role: Clerk of the Parliament for the Rump, in succession to Henry Elsynge, who withdrew around the time of the Purge
eyes.side: The purged House of Commons (the Rump)
eyes.where: House of Commons, St Stephen's Chapel, Westminster
eyes.vantage_label: the legislature that made the court
eyes.authenticity: The Commons Journal is the House's formal minute of orders and votes, printed in the eighteenth century and online at British History Online. It records decisions, not debate. The exact date Scobell took over from Elsynge is given here only approximately.
eyes.bio: The Journal is the paper spine of the revolution: the committee to prepare a charge, the claim to supreme power without King or Lords, the Act erecting the court, the audience given to the Dutch envoys pleading for the King's life, and the votes ending the monarchy and the House of Lords.

sources.title: House of Commons Journal vol. 6: 6 January 1649 (BHO)
House of Commons Journal vol. 6: 29 January 1649 (BHO)

eyes.name: Princess Elizabeth Stuart
eyes.role: Second daughter of Charles I, aged 13, in Parliament's custody with her brother Henry, Duke of Gloucester (8)
eyes.where: St James's Palace, brought from Syon House
eyes.vantage_label: the King's daughter at the last meeting
eyes.authenticity: Her short account headed 'What the King said to me, January 29, 1648[/9], being the last time I had the happiness to see him' survives and was printed in royalist collections soon afterwards. She says herself that she could not recall every word; it is a child's memorandum written within days, not a transcript.
eyes.bio: Elizabeth wrote down her father's last instructions: not to grieve, and to know that he had forgiven his enemies but that she should never trust them. She died a prisoner at Carisbrooke Castle in September 1650.

sources.title: Pan Macmillan history blog: The final hours of Charles I (quotes her account)

eyes.name: Sir Thomas Herbert
eyes.role: Traveller and writer; groom of the bedchamber placed with the captive King by Parliament, aged 42
eyes.side: Parliament's appointee who became the King's attendant
eyes.where: With the King at Hurst, Windsor, St James's and Whitehall
eyes.authenticity: Herbert wrote his account of the King's last two years about 1678–80, three decades on and under Charles II, when loyalty to the 'martyr king' was expected; it was printed in 1702 as 'Memoirs of the Two Last Years of the Reign of King Charles I'. Treat its details as recollection, not a contemporary record.
eyes.bio: Herbert was put in the King's service by Parliament and ended as one of his most devoted witnesses. His memoir supplies the domestic texture absent from the court record: the night before, the walk to Whitehall, the long wait in the cold.

eyes.name: Philip Henry
eyes.role: Westminster School pupil, aged 17, son of a Whitehall household servant; later a nonconformist minister
eyes.form: memoir (written later; recollection in his papers)
eyes.authenticity: The famous description of the groan is Henry's own later recollection, preserved in his papers (printed in M. H. Lee's 'Diaries and Letters of Philip Henry', 1882) and drawn on by his son Matthew Henry's 'Life' (1698). It was not written on the day.
eyes.bio: Henry had grown up within Whitehall, where his father served, and watched the King pass the family's door. His memory of the crowd's sound at the blow, and of troopers clearing the streets, is the most quoted bystander's account of the day.

sources.title: Diary of Philip Henry (extracts)

eyes.name: John Evelyn
eyes.role: Royalist gentleman and virtuoso, aged 28, living partly at Sayes Court, Deptford, his father-in-law's house
eyes.vantage_label: royalist in the same city, staying away
eyes.authenticity: Evelyn's 'Kalendarium' was compiled and revised from earlier notes, which is why an entry placed under 22 January 1649 already speaks of the execution on the 30th. First printed by William Bray in 1818; quotations here follow that modernised text.
eyes.bio: Evelyn went to hear the army preacher Hugh Peters urge the commissioners on in the Painted Chamber, but refused to watch the execution and kept the day as a fast. He wrote within reach of the event yet chose not to see it.

sources.title: John Evelyn's Diary 1649 (transcribed from Bray's edition)

eyes.name: Ralph Josselin
eyes.role: Vicar of Earls Colne, Essex, aged 31; former parliamentary army chaplain
eyes.authenticity: Autograph diary in private hands; edited by Alan Macfarlane (1976) and transcribed online by the Earls Colne records project (University of Cambridge).
eyes.bio: Josselin had supported Parliament, yet he wrote of the trial as strange and the execution as a 'black providence'. His entries show how news reached a market village: late, uncertain, and woven in with colds, sermons and his Hebrew studies.

sources.title: Earls Colne records: Diary of Ralph Josselin, 1649 index
Josselin, 31 January 1649
Josselin, 7 February 1649

eyes.name: Lucy Hutchinson
eyes.role: Poet and translator; wife of Colonel John Hutchinson, MP and a commissioner of the court who signed the death warrant
eyes.where: London, with her husband in Parliament
eyes.authenticity: The 'Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson' were written in the 1660s, after her husband's death in prison (1664), and first printed in 1806. A deliberate vindication of him, written when the regicides were being punished.
eyes.bio: Lucy Hutchinson gives the view from inside the court's own ranks: a commissioner who hesitated, sought guidance in prayer, and signed. Her husband escaped the scaffold at the Restoration but died a prisoner.

sources.title: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson (HathiTrust record)

eyes.name: John Playford
eyes.role: London bookseller and publisher at the Inner Temple, aged 25
eyes.where: His shop in the Inner Temple, London
eyes.authenticity: Playford published the authorised serial 'A Perfect Narrative of the Whole Proceedings of the High Court of Justice' and its continuations, issued within days of each sitting, and was one of the publishers of the scaffold speech. These were licensed publications that the regime allowed; they print the King's words but frame the proceedings as lawful.
eyes.bio: Within forty-eight hours of a sitting, Londoners could buy the speeches of the King, the Lord President and the Solicitor in print. Playford later became the leading music publisher of his age, issuing 'The English Dancing Master' in 1651.

sources.title: A continuation of the narrative ... Jan. 23 (Playford, 1649), Folger record
King Charls his speech ... (Cole, Tyton, Playford, 1649), Wellcome record

eyes.name: Alvise Contarini
eyes.role: Venetian diplomat, mediator at the peace congress of Münster that had just ended the Thirty Years War
eyes.vantage_label: abroad, at the Westphalian peace congress
eyes.authenticity: Dispatches to the Doge and Senate, calendared in English in the Calendar of State Papers, Venice, vol. 28 (online at British History Online). Dated in the Gregorian calendar; converted here to English Old Style for the timeline. Only the calendar's English summary has been used.
eyes.bio: Contarini passed on London newsletters to Venice and followed the Dutch attempt to save the King. His last word on the matter, that the King died 'like a common criminal' at his own subjects' hands, shows how Europe's diplomats received the news.

sources.title: CSP Venice vol. 28: January 1649 (BHO)
CSP Venice vol. 28: February 1649 (BHO)

eyes.name: Samuel Pepys
eyes.role: Pupil at St Paul's School in 1649, aged 15; by 1660 Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board
eyes.side: Then a boyish Roundhead; by 1660 a loyal servant of the restored Crown
eyes.where: Whitehall crowd (1649); Navy Office, Seething Lane (1660)
eyes.authenticity: Pepys's diary (1660–69) is in his own shorthand at Magdalene College, Cambridge; the 1 November 1660 entry recalls words he had spoken as a boy in 1649. Transcription online at pepysdiary.com from the Wheatley edition.
eyes.bio: Pepys did not begin his diary until 1660, but in it he admitted, with relief, that an old schoolfellow had left school before hearing the hard words young Pepys had said on the day of the execution. The entry shows how quickly 1649 became dangerous to remember.

sources.title: Pepys's diary, 1 November 1660

entries.headline: London news: the army ends the treaty and calls him 'Charles Stuart'
entries.digest: Contarini forwarded London advices reporting that the army's council had decided the negotiation with the King should end and that he should be brought to punishment. The newsletter remarked that he was now referred to simply as 'Charles Stuart'. The army had already purged the Commons on 6 December.
entries.source_note: CSP Venice vol. 28, no. 228–229 (letter of 22 Jan 1649 N.S. enclosing advices of 15 Dec 1648; calendar of the advices' style uncertain).

entries.headline: Committee of 38 named to prepare proceedings against the King
entries.digest: The purged House named a committee of thirty-eight members to consider how to proceed against the King. Some of those named were moderates who never attended; the work fell to a small group.
entries.source_note: History of Parliament blog (2019) citing the Commons Journal.

entries.headline: A commissioner hesitates, prays, and signs
entries.digest: Lucy Hutchinson wrote that her husband, named a commissioner, was very unwilling to take part, but after seeking God's guidance in prayer and finding no check on his conscience, he attended and signed. She wrote this years later, when signing had become a capital crime and she was defending his memory.
entries.source_note: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson (written c. 1664–71, printed 1806); passage paraphrased from the standard account, page not checked.

entries.headline: The Commons declare themselves the supreme power
entries.digest: After the Lords threw out the ordinance for the trial, the Commons resolved that the people are the original of all just power and that the Commons in Parliament, chosen by the people, hold the supreme power, their enactments binding without King or Lords. It was the legal hinge of the whole proceeding.
entries.quote: have the Supreme Power in this Nation
entries.source_note: Commons Journal 4 Jan 1649, as quoted in History of Parliament blog (2019).

entries.headline: A vicar notes the anniversary of the Five Members
entries.digest: Josselin spent the evening at a neighbour's, finished Baker's Chronicle and began a project of reconciling apparently conflicting scriptures. He noted that seven years before to the day the King had come to the House for the five members, and that now the Commons of themselves had ordered his trial. Many feared ruin; he wrote that if the work was of God it would stand, and if not it would fall.
entries.quote: the Commons of themselves, ordered the Trial of the King
entries.source_note: Josselin diary, 4 Jan 1649 (Earls Colne online transcription, entry 70003800).

entries.headline: The Act erecting a High Court of Justice passes
entries.digest: The Journal records the third reading and passing of the Act for erecting a High Court of Justice for the trial of the King, with no division recorded. The commissioners named in it were ordered to meet on the Monday at two in the afternoon in the Painted Chamber. Some 135 commissioners were named.
entries.source_note: Commons Journal vol. 6, 6 January 1649 (BHO node 18707); number named from History of Parliament blog.

entries.headline: First meeting: barely half the commissioners come
entries.digest: The court's journal opens with the first meeting of the commissioners in the Painted Chamber. Only about fifty-four of those named appeared. Several who were named, including Fairfax, came once or not at all; others, like Algernon Sidney, attended private sessions but never sat in Westminster Hall.
entries.source_note: History of Parliament blog (2019), from the court journal (Nalson 1684).

entries.date_display: January 1648/9 (chosen c. 10 January, in the chair by 12 January)
entries.headline: An obscure lawyer becomes Lord President
entries.digest: With senior judges declining to serve, the commissioners chose John Bradshaw as their president. He took up the role in the following days and became the court's single voice in its exchanges with the King.
entries.source_note: The National Archives blog gives 12 January for his appointment; other accounts date his election to 10 January.

entries.headline: Hearing Hugh Peters urge the commissioners on
entries.digest: Evelyn went to Westminster and heard the army preacher Hugh Peters exhort the commissioners gathered in the Painted Chamber to proceed against the King. Evelyn, a royalist, called them all rebels.
entries.quote: I heard the rebel, Peters, incite the rebel powers
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary, 17 Jan 1648/9 (Bray text).

entries.headline: Nearly drowned when the wherries collide at night
entries.digest: Returning by river, Evelyn's boat fouled another in the dark and he came close to drowning. Ordinary danger runs alongside public drama in his pages that week.
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary, 19 Jan 1648/9 (Bray text).

entries.headline: The Dutch send an envoy; the sentence 'will doubtless be capital'
entries.digest: Contarini reported that the Prince of Wales had asked the States General to send someone to save his father's life, and that they had chosen Adriaan Pauw. He wrote that the process was believed already drawn up and that the sentence, though not yet passed, would doubtless be capital.
entries.source_note: CSP Venice vol. 28, no. 232 (letter dated 29 Jan 1649 N.S.).

entries.headline: The King brought from Windsor to London
entries.digest: Herbert recalled the King's removal under guard from Windsor to St James's Palace on the eve of the trial, and the reduced household around him. He wrote this decades later.
entries.source_note: Herbert, Memoirs (written 1678–80, printed 1702); date of the removal standard in trial accounts.

entries.headline: The court sits in public; the charge is read
entries.digest: The journal records the court's procession into Westminster Hall, the roll of commissioners, the King brought in, and the charge exhibited by the Solicitor and read by the clerk. It minutes the King's refusal to answer and the adjournment. During the roll call a voice from a gallery interrupted when Fairfax's name was called; the journal itself names no speaker.
entries.source_note: Court journal as printed by Nalson (1684); interruption as reported in trial narratives.

entries.headline: 'By what power am I called hither?'
entries.digest: Kept with his hat on before the court, Charles demanded to know by what lawful authority he had been brought there, reminding the court he had been negotiating a treaty with Parliament on the Isle of Wight. He said he would not betray the trust given him by God and the ancient laws by answering a new, unlawful authority.
entries.quote: I would know by what power I am called hither
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684) and the authorised 'Perfect Narrative' (Playford, 1649).

entries.headline: 'In the name of the people of England'
entries.digest: Bradshaw answered that the King was called to answer by the authority of the Commons of England assembled in Parliament, on behalf of the people of England, by whom he had been elected king. Charles retorted that England had never been an elective kingdom. Bradshaw adjourned the court.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); 'Perfect Narrative' (1649).

entries.headline: The Solicitor exhibits the charge of tyranny and treason
entries.digest: Cook stood to present the charge in the name of the people of England: that Charles, trusted with a limited power to govern by law, had made war on Parliament and people and was guilty of the bloodshed, a tyrant, traitor and murderer. When he rose to speak, the King tried to stop him.
entries.source_note: Charge in the court journal (Nalson 1684).

entries.headline: His translation 'Liberty and Servitude' comes out
entries.digest: Evelyn noted the publication of his translation 'Of Liberty and Servitude', adding that he had been severely threatened over its preface. Even a translation's preface was dangerous that week.
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary, 21 Jan 1648/9 (Bray text).

entries.headline: Second refusal: 'the liberty of the people'
entries.digest: On the second public day Charles again refused to plead, saying it was not his case alone but the freedom and liberty of the people of England that he defended, for if power without law could make laws no subject was safe. He had prepared written reasons against the court's jurisdiction; they were not allowed to be delivered and were printed afterwards.
entries.source_note: Court journal and 'Perfect Narrative'; the paper of reasons printed 1649 (date of printing not checked).

entries.headline: Cook asks that the charge be taken as confessed
entries.digest: Cook asked the court that, if the prisoner still would not answer, his refusal be recorded and the charge taken as confessed, so that judgment could follow. In law, a prisoner standing mute could be treated as admitting the charge.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); wording not checked against the printed text.

entries.headline: Thames frozen; a fast kept for the King's death
entries.digest: Under 22 January Evelyn recorded the Thames frozen over and violent winds, then added that the rebels went on to try, condemn and murder the King on the 30th, which so horrified him that he kept the day of the execution as a fast and would not be present. The entry was evidently written up after the event.
entries.quote: I kept the day of his martyrdom a fast
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary, entry under 22 Jan 1648/9 (Bray text).

entries.headline: The trial in print within two days
entries.digest: Playford issued 'A continuation of the narrative', covering the court's sitting in Westminster Hall on 23 January with the speeches of the King, the Lord President and the Solicitor-General. The imprint is dated 25 January 1648 — Old Style for 1649. The series was licensed and gave the public the King's own objections in his own words, inside a frame that treated the court as lawful.
entries.source_note: Folger catalogue record 141680: imprint 'Printed for John Playford ... Jan. 25. 1648'.

entries.headline: Third refusal recorded as a default
entries.digest: The journal records that the King refused a third time to answer, and that the clerk was directed to record his default. The court then withdrew and did not bring him into the Hall again until the 27th.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); not checked page by page.

entries.headline: Witnesses heard in private
entries.digest: Since the King would not plead, the commissioners heard witnesses in the Painted Chamber rather than in open court: some thirty men who testified to seeing the King in arms at Nottingham, Edgehill, Naseby and elsewhere. Their depositions are minuted in the journal.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); number of witnesses as usually given, not counted.

entries.headline: The commissioners settle the sentence
entries.digest: In closed session the commissioners resolved that the King should be condemned as a tyrant, traitor, murderer and public enemy and put to death, and had the sentence engrossed to be read the next day.
entries.source_note: The National Archives blog (26 January decision), from the court journal.

entries.headline: Pauw hurrying via Calais 'to prevent the death'
entries.digest: Contarini reported that the Dutch ambassador extraordinary Pauw was making for London by way of Calais as fast as possible to prevent the King's death. An enclosed London newsletter told how the King had been brought before judges three days, disputing their authority, and how the court had ignored a letter from the French ambassador.
entries.source_note: CSP Venice vol. 28 (letter dated 5 Feb 1649 N.S. and enclosed London advices).

entries.headline: He asks to be heard by Lords and Commons
entries.digest: Brought in for the last time, Charles asked to be heard by the Lords and Commons in the Painted Chamber before sentence, saying he had something to propose for the peace of the kingdom. The court withdrew to consider and refused. After the sentence was read he tried to speak and was taken away, protesting that he was not suffered to speak.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); 'Perfect Narrative' (1649).

entries.headline: The Lord President's speech and the sentence
entries.digest: Bradshaw delivered a long address arguing from law and history that kings are under the law and answerable to their people, citing deposed kings of England and Scotland. The clerk then read the sentence: that Charles Stuart, as a tyrant, traitor, murderer and public enemy, be put to death by severing his head from his body. The commissioners stood to signify assent.
entries.quote: a Tyrrant, Traytor, a Murtherer, and a Publique Enemy
entries.source_note: Sentence as quoted on The National Archives blog; speech in the court journal (Nalson 1684).

entries.headline: Sentence pronounced; a disturbance in the gallery
entries.digest: The journal records the sentence read and the court's adjournment. During the proceedings a woman in a gallery called out against the charge's claim to speak for all the people of England; later accounts identify her as Lady Fairfax, the Lord General's wife, but give her words in differing versions.
entries.source_note: Court journal (Nalson 1684); identification and wording from later narratives, which differ.

entries.headline: 'What the King said to me'
entries.digest: Elizabeth set down her father's words at their last meeting. He told her not to grieve or torment herself for him. He had forgiven his enemies, but she should never trust them. He told her brother Henry not to let himself be made king while his elder brothers lived; the boy answered that he would be torn in pieces first.
entries.quote: He wished me not to grieve or torment myself for him
entries.source_note: Elizabeth's account as quoted in Pan Macmillan history blog.

entries.headline: The children's visit, remembered
entries.digest: Herbert later described the King taking leave of his two youngest children, giving them small jewels and blessing them, and the princess's weeping. His account, written decades later, broadly matches Elizabeth's own.
entries.source_note: Herbert, Memoirs (written 1678–80, printed 1702).

entries.headline: The Dutch ambassadors plead for the King
entries.digest: Letters from the States General were read in French and English, and the House gave the ambassadors Pauw and Joachimi an audience that afternoon, with chairs and carpets set for them on the north side. Pauw read their requests in French; the Speaker said he would report them, and the envoys withdrew. The warrant for execution, signed by fifty-nine commissioners, bears this same date.
entries.source_note: Commons Journal vol. 6, 29 January 1649 (BHO node 18726); warrant date and signatures from Parliamentary Archives (HL/PO/JO/10/1/297A).

entries.headline: The last morning
entries.digest: Herbert recalled the King rising early, asking for warm clothes so that the cold should not make him shiver and be taken for fear, praying with Bishop Juxon, walking through St James's Park under guard to Whitehall, and a long wait before being called out to the scaffold in the afternoon.
entries.source_note: Herbert, Memoirs (written 1678–80, printed 1702).

entries.headline: The scaffold speech
entries.digest: With the crowd held back by soldiers, Charles spoke mainly to those on the scaffold. He declared himself innocent of beginning the war, forgave those who had brought him to death, and said the people's liberty lay in having government and laws, not a share in government: a subject and a sovereign were different things. He died, he said, a Christian of the Church of England, going from a corruptible to an incorruptible crown.
entries.quote: a subject and a sovereign are clean different things
entries.source_note: King Charls his speech made upon the scaffold (London, 1649); 'corruptible to an incorruptible Crown' also quoted in Pan Macmillan blog.

entries.headline: The groan of the crowd
entries.digest: Henry, who had come to London to see his father and stayed at Whitehall, watched the King pass by. At the blow, he recalled, the thousands present gave a groan he never wished to hear again. Troops then marched both ways from Charing Cross to Westminster to scatter the crowd, and he had trouble getting home unhurt.
entries.quote: as I never heard before & desire I may never hear again
entries.source_note: Philip Henry's recollection, as printed in his diaries and letters (ed. Lee, 1882); later recollection, not a same-day entry.

entries.headline: No one to be proclaimed king
entries.digest: On the day of the execution the Commons passed an Act forbidding anyone to proclaim a new King of England, so that the Prince of Wales could not be declared Charles II at the moment of his father's death.
entries.source_note: Act prohibiting the proclaiming of any person to be King, 30 Jan 1649 (Acts and Ordinances of the Interregnum); not checked in the Journal text.

entries.headline: A rumour of the execution, on a cold fast day
entries.digest: Josselin wrote that he had heard the King was executed, though he was not certain of it. He noted that the King had been sentenced on 27 January, Bradshaw as Lord President pronouncing it. The day was a fast and very cold, and he supposed fasts would soon be laid down since people neglected them.
entries.source_note: Josselin diary, 31 Jan 1649 (Earls Colne online, entry 70003870).

entries.headline: 'King Charls his Case': the speech never given
entries.digest: Cook published the argument he would have made had the King pleaded, as an appeal to all rational men. It sets out the case that a king who wages war on his people forfeits his trust, and adds charges about the death of James I, the loss of La Rochelle and the blood of Ireland. It is the prosecution's case written for readers after the verdict.
entries.source_note: King Charls his Case (London, 1649), EEBO-TCP A34423 (Oxford Text Archive record); month of issue not checked.

entries.headline: The scaffold speech goes on sale
entries.digest: The scaffold speech, with a relation of the King's going to execution, was printed 'by special authority' for Peter Cole, Francis Tyton and John Playford. Its title page dates the execution 'Tuesday the 30 of Jan. 1648', Old Style. Licensed printing put the King's last words in circulation alongside the regime's narratives of the trial.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection record xs8p7h4d; exact day of issue not checked.

entries.headline: The 'New Court of Injustice' tries the royalist lords
entries.digest: Evelyn recorded the trial of the Duke of Hamilton, the Earl of Norwich and Lord Capel before what he called the rebels' New Court of Injustice — another High Court of Justice, set up on the model of the King's.
entries.quote: the rebels' New Court of Injustice
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary, 1 Feb 1648/9 (Bray text).

entries.headline: 'Fear and tremble at it oh England'
entries.digest: Nursing a cold, Josselin wrote that he was much troubled by the 'black providence' of the King's death and by his own vain thoughts, and that people everywhere were passionately discussing it. He recorded that the Commons had debated kings and peers on Monday, voted the Lords abolished on Tuesday, and on Wednesday voted to lay aside government by a king for a council of state.
entries.quote: fear and tremble at it oh England
entries.source_note: Josselin diary, 7 Feb 1649 (Earls Colne online, entry 70003880).

entries.headline: Kingship voted unnecessary and dangerous
entries.digest: The Commons resolved that the office of a king in the nation was unnecessary, burdensome and dangerous to the liberty, safety and interest of the people, and should be abolished, the day after voting the House of Lords useless and dangerous.
entries.source_note: Commons Journal 6–7 Feb 1649 (dates confirmed by Josselin's 7 Feb entry); wording not checked in the Journal.

entries.headline: An old man dies 'before troubles'
entries.digest: Riding home from a visit with his wife, Josselin heard that Edward Cressener had died suddenly, old and worn out, before the troubles he had greatly feared. Public fear enters a private obituary.
entries.quote: before troubles which he very much feared
entries.source_note: Josselin diary, 13 Feb 1649 (Earls Colne online, entry 70003890).

entries.headline: 'Like a common criminal'
entries.digest: Contarini wrote to Venice that the King had at last lost crown and life by the executioner's hand in London, like a common criminal, with no one speaking in his favour, and condemned by his own subjects. He enclosed a copy of the scaffold speech.
entries.source_note: CSP Venice vol. 28, Contarini to the Doge and Senate, 26 Feb 1649 N.S.

entries.headline: The lords beheaded in Palace Yard
entries.digest: Evelyn noted that the royalist lords tried before the new court were now executed in Palace Yard, Westminster. Hamilton, Holland and Capel died; Norwich was reprieved.
entries.quote: Now were the Lords murdered in the Palace Yard
entries.source_note: Evelyn diary (Bray text); the editor notes the entry was dated 5 March in the original while the executions were on 9 March.

entries.headline: The Act abolishing the kingly office
entries.digest: The Commons passed the Act abolishing the office of king, declaring that it had been found by experience unnecessary, burdensome and dangerous. England was declared a Commonwealth in May.
entries.source_note: Act for the abolishing the kingly office, 17 Mar 1649 (Acts and Ordinances of the Interregnum); not checked in the Journal text.

entries.headline: Afraid of what he said as a boy
entries.digest: Meeting his old schoolfellow Mr Christmas, Pepys was reminded that he had been a great Roundhead as a boy. He feared Christmas might remember what he had said the day the King was beheaded — that if he were to preach on him his text would be 'the memory of the wicked shall rot' — but found the friend had left school before that. Only weeks earlier, ten regicides had been executed in London.
entries.quote: The memory of the wicked shall rot
entries.source_note: Pepys's diary, 1 Nov 1660 (pepysdiary.com).

claims.claim: Purged Commons names a committee of 38 to prepare proceedings against the King
claims.evidence: Commons Journal, via History of Parliament blog (2019)

claims.claim: Commons resolve they hold 'the Supreme Power in this Nation' without King or Lords
Act for erecting a High Court of Justice for trial of the King passed on third reading
First meeting of commissioners in the Painted Chamber; about 54 of c.135 attend
claims.evidence: Court journal (Nalson 1684), via History of Parliament

claims.claim: Charge exhibited: the King as tyrant, traitor and murderer who levied war on Parliament and people
King refuses to plead, demanding by what lawful authority he is tried
Interruptions from a gallery, attributed in later accounts to Lady Fairfax; her words survive only in differing later versions
claims.evidence: Later trial narratives and histories; not established in the clerks' minutes

claims.claim: Some thirty witnesses depose in private that they saw the King in arms against Parliament
Sentence: death as 'a Tyrrant, Traytor, a Murtherer, and a Publique Enemy'
claims.evidence: Court journal; quoted by The National Archives

claims.claim: Dutch ambassadors Pauw and Joachimi given audience in the Commons to plead for the King
The King tells his daughter he has forgiven his enemies but she must never trust them
claims.evidence: Elizabeth's written account of the last meeting

claims.claim: On the scaffold: innocent of starting the war; 'a subject and a sovereign are clean different things'
claims.evidence: King Charls his speech made upon the scaffold (1649)

claims.claim: Essex vicar hears of the execution but is not sure it is true
Prosecutor prints the argument he could not deliver because the King never pleaded
Venetian diplomat reports the King died 'like a common criminal' with none speaking for him
Act abolishing the kingly office passed
claims.evidence: Acts and Ordinances of the Interregnum

convergences.label: The Commons claim supreme power
convergences.note: The Journal records a constitutional revolution in one resolution; in Essex, Josselin heard only that the Commons 'of themselves' had ordered a trial, and set it beside the anniversary of the King's own raid on the House in 1642.

convergences.label: Eve of the trial
convergences.note: As the King was moved to St James's, Evelyn was nearly drowned on the Thames, and at Münster Contarini was already writing that the sentence would doubtless be capital.

convergences.label: First public day in Westminster Hall
convergences.note: Four voices in one room, all recorded by the court's side: the prosecutor's charge, the King's demand to know by what power, the President's answer in the name of the people, and the clerk's minute of a refusal.

convergences.label: Second refusal; a diary written after the fact
convergences.note: While Charles argued in the Hall that his cause was the people's liberty, Evelyn's entry under the same date already looks ahead to the execution — a reminder that his 'diary' was composed later.

convergences.label: Sentence
convergences.note: The President's long speech, the King's unheeded request to address Parliament, the clerk's minute — and four days later a country vicar, writing the date down correctly but unsure whether the King was yet dead.

convergences.label: Last day: children, envoys, warrant
convergences.note: In the same hours that the princess heard her father's last advice, the Commons gave a ceremonial audience to Dutch envoys pleading for his life, and the warrant bore its date.

convergences.label: The execution at Whitehall
convergences.note: The King's speech, a schoolboy's memory of the groan, a servant's memory of the cold morning, a royalist who stayed at home fasting, and a House passing an act against proclaiming a successor.

convergences.label: The monarchy voted down
convergences.note: Josselin's diary gives the days of the votes on the Lords and on kingship as precisely as the Journal, and adds what the Journal leaves out: that people everywhere were talking of nothing else.

ties.note: The two principal speakers of the trial: Bradshaw insisted on the people's authority, Charles denied the court existed.
Cook drew and presented the charge; because Charles never pleaded, Cook printed the speech he could not make.
Phelps was clerk to the court over which Bradshaw presided; the trial volume came to be called 'Bradshaw's Journal'.
Father and daughter; her account is the only record of their last conversation by one of the two people present.
Herbert attended the King daily from Hurst Castle to the scaffold.
Both were in the room at St James's on 29 January; their two accounts, one written within days and one decades later, can be read side by side.
Lucy Hutchinson's husband sat as a commissioner under Bradshaw and signed the warrant.
Playford published the King's words from the trial and, with Cole and Tyton, his scaffold speech.
Both kept the century's great London diaries and became friends after the Restoration; in 1649 one stayed away from the execution and the other, a schoolboy, approved of it.
Cook was executed as a regicide in October 1660 and appears in Pepys's diary in the weeks when Pepys feared his own boyhood words of 1649 might be remembered.
Contarini's dispatches followed the Dutch envoy Pauw's mission, which the Commons Journal records reaching the House on 29 January.
Josselin's diary names Bradshaw as the Lord President who pronounced sentence.

threads_out.note: Contarini wrote from Münster, where he had mediated the Peace of Westphalia signed in October 1648, three months before the trial; Charles's sister Elizabeth, the 'Winter Queen' of Bohemia, had been at the centre of the war's first crisis.
John Evelyn and Samuel Pepys, who recorded 1649 (one at the time, one in recollection), are the two great diarists of the Great Fire of London seventeen years later.
Westminster Hall, where Charles I was tried in 1649, was the same hall in which Warren Hastings was impeached before the Lords from 1788.
When the National Convention tried Louis XVI in 1792–93, the trial and execution of Charles I was the precedent that deputies and the King's defenders on both sides invoked.
